title: Generic Swap
story: Two boxes got mixed up at the warehouse — the 'Fragile' package and the 'Books' package are in each other's spots. You need a function that can swap ANY two items. Not just boxes, not just strings — ANY two values of the same type.
why: Generic functions operate on any type, letting you write algorithms once — swap, compare, transform — and apply them to Int, Str, Bool, or your own custom types.
analogy: A generic function is like a universal remote — the same buttons (code) work with any brand of TV (type). You program the remote once, and it controls Samsung, Sony, or LG — just like `duplicate[T]` works with `Vec[Int]`, `Vec[Str]`, or `Vec[Bool]`.
try_it: Write a `wrap_all[T](items: &Vec[T]) -> Vec[Box[T]]` function that wraps every item in a Box. Then write `unwrap_all[T](boxes: &Vec[Box[T]]) -> Vec[T]` that extracts all values. Use the Box type from the previous lesson. Test with both Int and Str vectors.
tips: Generic functions declare `[T]` after the function name: `fn my_func[T](...)` — T can be any type
The same generic function works with different types as long as the operations are valid for all of them
`.push()` and `.get()` work on `Vec[T]` for any T — the Vec operations don't care what T is
common_mistakes: Forgetting `[T]` before the parameters: `fn pair_them(first: T, second: T)` won't compile without `[T]`
Trying to mix types in a single call — `pair_them(1, "hi")` fails because T must be one type per call
Assuming all types support `==` or `+` — generic functions can only use operations that work for ALL types
